content: OMA1, also known as mitochondrial metalloendopeptidase OMA1, is an enzyme encoded by the OMA1 gene in humans. This protein functions as a metalloprotease and is a critical component of the quality control system within the inner mitochondrial membrane. It is activated by the pro-apoptotic proteins Bax and Bak, and upon activation, OMA1 facilitates the release of cytochrome c, which subsequently triggers the process of apoptosis. Structure The OMA1 gene encodes a metalloprotease that belongs to a conserved family of membrane-embedded metallopeptidases found in mitochondria. The protein has a molecular weight of approximately 1 kDa and consists of 524 amino acids, including a mitochondrial targeting sequence located at positions 1–13. Function Within the inner mitochondrial membrane, there are two types of AAA proteases: m-AAA protease and i-AAA protease. These proteases are named based on their orientation within the membrane. The m-AAA protease faces the mitochondrial matrix, while the i-AAA protease faces the intermembrane space. OMA1 has been shown to share overlapping proteolytic activity with the m-AAA protease. However, unlike the m-AAA protease, OMA1 does not fully regulate the turnover of certain substrates, such as Oxidase Assembly 1 (Oxa1). Instead, OMA1 generates N-terminal and C-terminal proteolytic fragments of its substrates. OMA1 also plays a role in the regulation of the mitochondrial inner membrane fusion protein OPA1. When mitochondria experience a loss of membrane potential or a depletion of adenosine triphosphate (ATP), OMA1 degrades OPA1. This inducible proteolysis serves as a regulatory mechanism to inactivate OPA1 proteolytically, thereby preventing the fusion of the mitochondrial network. Clinical Significance OMA1 appears to have a role in neurodegeneration. Mutations in the OMA1 gene have been identified in patients with Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), suggesting a potential link between OMA1 dysfunction and the pathogenesis of this neurodegenerative disease.
